_readme: THE SCREEN REGISTER — [pipeline C-13] Private/company/pipeline/02-shared-chassis.md
The complete set of NON-APP-SPECIFIC screens: the ones that are the same in all fifty apps and
therefore ship in the chassis rather than being written per app. Sourced from DoD §4-A.
WHY A REGISTER AND NOT A CHECKLIST IN PROSE. C-13's acceptance is that a NAMED LIST is declared and
the app_brick probe asserts each screen is present in a fresh stamp. A list nobody can check is how
an account-deletion button sat doing nothing for months while passing every check the repo had.
STATUS values:
present  - it exists in the chassis; `anchor` names the file and the symbol that prove it
blocked  - it CANNOT be built yet; `blockedBy` names what has to land first, and that claim is
checked (a blocker that has already shipped fails the build, so nothing hides behind
a stale excuse)
todo     - buildable now, not yet built. Counted and PRINTED on every run.
Enforced by tooling/ci/assert-screen-set.mjs.
ANCHOR KINDS. `anchor.kind` says what the symbol IS, because a bare word match is the
declaration-vs-usage trap: renaming `class NotFoundScreen` to `class NotFoundScreenGone` left the
guard green, since the class's own constructor still matched the bare name.
class  (default) - our own widget/class; matches the DECLARATION
member           - a method we own
uses             - a Flutter widget we use rather than declare (SegmentedButton, AboutListTile)
STATUS `not-building` — a fourth state, added 2026-07-29. It means: this screen was CONSIDERED and
deliberately not built, with the reason recorded. It is not `todo` (nobody is coming back to it) and
not `blocked` (nothing is in the way). Every entry names why building it would produce a DEAD
FEATURE — a language picker with one locale, a profile form that saves nowhere — which is the shape
[2]C-6 exists to catch. A deliberate no is worth more than a permanent todo.
⚠️ A SUPERSEDED `todo` IS THE ONE DRIFT THIS GUARD CANNOT CATCH GENERICALLY. `firstrun.screens` sat
here as a todo after both of its halves had been split out into `firstrun.permission-priming`
(present) and `firstrun.splash-onboarding` (not-building) — a stale entry that read as outstanding
work. Nothing mechanical distinguishes it from a real todo, so WHEN YOU SPLIT AN ENTRY, DELETE THE
ORIGINAL in the same edit. Found 2026-07-29 by reading the list, not by running it.
🔴 THREE ENTRIES WERE MOVED BACK FROM `not-building` TO `todo` ON 2026-07-29, after the owner asked
what was actually blocking them. Each original reason stated a SYMPTOM as a CAUSE — "no profile data
model", "content is app-specific", "no users to ask" — and none survived checking. The language
picker was the fourth and is now built. THE RULE: a `not-building` entry must name what would
un-block it, and that un-blocker must be genuinely hard. If it is one file, it is a todo.

screens.what: A friendly screen when a widget throws during build, instead of Flutter's grey/red default.

reachable.why: installed before runApp, so an error in the FIRST build is already covered

screens.what: 404 for a route that does not resolve. Matters most on web, where a user can type a URL or follow a stale link.

reachable.why: without it go_router shows its own error page, which names internal route patterns

screens.what: Tells the user the network could not be reached. Driven by a FAILED REQUEST, not a connectivity plugin — knowing the radio is on says nothing about whether the API is reachable.

reachable.why: 🔴 THIS ENTRY CARRIED NO `reachable` AT ALL UNTIL 2026-08-06, AND THE WIDGET HAD ZERO CONSUMERS ANYWHERE IN THE REPOSITORY — its declaration and its constructor were the only two occurrences, and `offlineMessage` sat in both ARB files with nothing reading it. So the screen was present, anchored, green, and unreachable by every user of every stamped app: the [2]C-6 shape, arrived at by the guard treating a missing field as nothing to check. The banner is driven by a FAILED REQUEST (the config transport's own result, reported in BOTH directions) and never by a connectivity plugin — the radio being on says nothing about whether the API answers. It returns its child untouched while reachable, so the widget tree is unchanged until something has actually failed

screens.what: The kill-switch wall when the running version is below min_supported_version.

reachable.why: mounted in MaterialApp's builder, above the router

screens.what: The DPDP analytics consent question. THE single piece that turns the whole analytics rail on.

reachable.why: [2]C-6: the recorder had ZERO call sites and every event was silently discarded, and no test went red because refusing is the correct behaviour when consent is absent

screens.what: The settings screen itself.

reachable.why: a screen no route reaches is one no user can open

screens.what: Light/dark/system choice, persisted.

reachable.why: the control and the thing it controls are in DIFFERENT FILES, which is the whole reason presence cannot stand in for reachability here: the picker can render, store the choice and rebuild perfectly while MaterialApp silently defaults to ThemeMode.system, and the only symptom is that nothing changes colour. Identical in shape to `settings.language`, whose `locale:` line carries the same note

screens.what: Opens a support email with the app name pre-filled.

reachable.why: the anchor is a `member`, and that pattern (`_contactSupport\s*\(`) matches the method's OWN DECLARATION — so deleting the tile that calls it leaves the anchor green while E1's mandated support contact becomes unreachable from inside the app. The call site is a TEAR-OFF with no parentheses, which is precisely why it needs its own assertion: no `symbol(` pattern can see it

screens.what: Delete the account and its data, with re-authentication first.

reachable.why: its confirm button called Navigator.pop and NOTHING else until 2026-07-28 — a store-compliance defect that passed every check the repo had

screens.what: Standard about dialog with version and legalese.

reachable.why: 🔴 THE ONE OF THE FOUR WHOSE ANCHOR IS ALSO ITS CALL SITE — `AboutListTile(` is a Flutter widget we USE, so there is no separate caller to point at, and an honest second assertion has to ask a different question rather than restate the first. The question is whether the dialog it opens carries anything ACTIONABLE. It did not: `applicationVersion` was absent until 2026-08-06, and `showAboutDialog` renders no version line rather than complaining, so a complete-looking dialog told a user reporting a bug nothing about which build they were running. It reads the RUNNING version (`packageVersionProvider`), not the compiled-in `String.fromEnvironment` default a build that forgot its --dart-define would report as truth

screens.what: The paywall: plans priced by the rail, a hosted checkout, and the honest refusal where a store forbids one.
screens.detail: BUILT 2026-08-01 ([pipeline 5]M-6). It was blocked until the purchase path existed, and that was the right call — a paywall with no way to pay is a fail-closed seam with no proven open path. What unblocked it is the whole path landing at once: packages/purchases (offerings from the rail config, the hosted-checkout launcher, the bounded convergence poller), the shared entitlement read, and the ROSCA cancel call.

reachable.why: the screen is reached from the PaywallGate's upgrade button AND from Settings; the route is what makes either possible, and it is also the step-count source assert-purchase-path.mjs derives ROSCA from

screens.what: See the plan's state, restore it on a new device, and cancel it — one tap from Settings.
screens.detail: [pipeline 5]M-9 (ROSCA) and M-10 (restore). Cancelling reaches POST /v1/plan/cancel — a REAL server call that writes an append-only record of the request, not a mailto: link. The screen reports four distinct outcomes because `recorded` and `executed` are separately true, and collapsing them would have the app tell a user their subscription is over while the billing continues.

reachable.why: the account-deletion dialog's confirm button in this same chassis once called Navigator.pop and NOTHING else, which looks exactly like a button that worked. A cancel button that does not reach the rail is the same defect where it costs money

screens.what: Opening / PENDING / unlocked / refused — the four states a hosted checkout can leave the app in.
screens.detail: 🔴 PENDING IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS WHY THIS IS ITS OWN REGISTER ROW. A hosted checkout returns the buyer the instant they press pay; the merchant of record's notification reaches our server afterwards. So there is a real window in which the user HAS paid and the server does NOT know, and the two obvious answers are both wrong: unlocking on the return unlocks abandoned checkouts and declined cards, and showing 'purchase failed' tells a paying customer their money vanished. The client re-reads with BOUNDED backoff (kCheckoutConvergenceDelays — five attempts, a portfolio constraint, not a UX preference) and lands in a stated terminal state.

reachable.why: an enum of states nothing ever enters is a switch statement, not a screen. The pending branch is the one a user with money in flight actually sees

screens.what: Sign-in, sign-up and forgot-password, plus the redirect guard that gates every other route.

reachable.why: the REDIRECT GUARD is what makes these screens reachable — screens do not navigate after sign-in themselves, because pushing from both places leaves two routes racing to be top of the stack. 🔴 CORRECTED 2026-07-29: that was true about getting IN and false about getting OUT. `redirect` re-runs when the router is TOLD to, and nothing watched `authStateChanges()`, so a stamped app signed the user in and went on showing them the form they had just completed. This pattern matched throughout — PRESENCE IS NOT ENFORCEMENT, and no single grep can prove a screen can be left. The exit is proven instead by the `auth-redirect-follows-session` property, which drives the real form; found by running it, not by reading it.

screens.what: The OAuth callback — the screen a browser redirect lands on. 🔻 NARROWED 2026-08-11: this entry used to also cover password reset, which now has its own `auth.password-reset` row because it shipped. ⚠️ It also still names email verification, and that claim is STALE in the other direction — `VerifyEmailScreen` shipped 2026-08-09 and is reached by the router's own gate rather than by a link. Left as found rather than silently corrected by an increment that does not own it; flagged so the next pass on this register fixes it deliberately.
screens.detail: Entered by following a browser redirect back into a NATIVE binary, which is the half `app_links` is genuinely required for. `app_links` 7.2.1 supports all six platforms (verified against pub.dev 2026-07-28) and would earn its place under [2]C-4 as native-binary — it ships platform code — but it is not a dependency yet, and no target here registers a URI scheme. ⚠️ Web carries two traps recorded in AuthCapabilities: the token arrives in the URL FRAGMENT so query parsing fails SILENTLY, and app_links on web reports only the INITIAL link.

screens.what: Set a new password — where the emailed reset link lands.
screens.detail: 🔴 SPLIT OUT OF `auth.callbacks` BECAUSE IT NO LONGER NEEDS DEEP LINKS. `app_links` is required to catch a redirect back into a NATIVE binary; on web the SDK reads `?code=` off the query itself, so the whole flow completes with no new dependency. That is why this row can be `present` while its former parent stays `blocked`. Before 2026-08-11 `sendPasswordReset` was implemented and a real recovery mail had been delivered (2026-08-03) with NO `updatePassword` on the seam, no route, and no `redirectTo` — help that could be asked for and not accepted. ⚠️ PKCE keeps the code verifier in the installation that REQUESTED the link, so a link opened on a second device cannot complete the exchange; the screen's dead-link state is the answer to that, not a workaround for it. 🔴 AND THAT STATE WAS UNREACHABLE FROM THE FAILURE IT EXPLAINS UNTIL 2026-08-11: the only thing that routed to this screen was the SUCCESS event, so an expired or cross-device link landed on `/` and was bounced to `/sign-in`, and the same arrival with a `?code=` and no verifier CRASHED (GlitchTip SUBLY-8, fatal, uncaught out of runZonedGuarded). Both halves now land here: the redirect carries an `nk_auth=reset` marker in the QUERY, which gotrue preserves on its failure redirect while REPLACING the fragment (measured live against the project on 2026-08-11), and the seam turns the stream error into `AuthEventKind.recoveryLinkFailed`. ⚠️ OWNER/INTEGRATOR ACTION, NOT CODE: the exact redirect the build now sends is `https://<origin>/?nk_auth=reset#/reset-password` and it must stay on the project's redirect allow-list — a redirect that is not on it does not error, gotrue silently substitutes the Site URL, so a misconfigured list is indistinguishable from a working one.

reachable.why: the REDIRECT GUARD is what reaches this screen, and it is reached from an EVENT rather than from a URL — which is the whole reason this row exists. A recovery session is an ordinary session (same user, same token, same emission on `authStateChanges`), so the guard cannot infer it; `authEvents()` carries `AuthEventKind.passwordRecovery` and `passwordRecoveryProvider` holds it — and the FAILURE half is reached the same way, from `passwordResetArrivalProvider`, which reads the launch URL's marker and the seam's `recoveryLinkFailed` event. ⚠️ PRESENCE IS NOT ENFORCEMENT and this pattern proves only that the guard names the route: that the gate actually FIRES, and that `routerRefreshProvider` re-runs it when the event lands with nobody navigating, is proven by driving the real router in `apps/subly/test/password_reset_test.dart` — found by running it, not by reading it.

screens.what: Ends the session on this device.

reachable.why: placed ABOVE account deletion — it is the action a user wants hundreds of times more often, and putting the irreversible one first invites a misfire. Re-pointed 2026-08-11 from `ref.read(authRepositoryProvider).signOut()`: that call was fire-and-forget, so the deliberate throw from SecureSessionStorage.removePersistedSession went nowhere and the per-user state on the device outlived the session. The two halves are split on purpose — `anchor` proves the handler reaches the real path (`signOutAndForgetUser(`), this proves the CONTROL reaches the handler. Anchoring both on the handler was measured and rejected: reverting the tile to the fire-and-forget call left the handler in place with nothing calling it, and every check stayed green

screens.what: Reminder toggle, gated on what the platform can actually do.

reachable.why: [2]C-7 earning its keep in real UI: on Linux the plugin shows but cannot schedule, and on Windows (pinned 17.x) it does neither. An honest sentence replaces the toggle there, because a switch that silently does nothing is worse than no switch

screens.what: Privacy policy and terms of service, reachable in-app.

reachable.why: both stores require these to be reachable IN-APP, not only from a store listing

screens.what: Explains why a permission is wanted BEFORE the OS prompt appears.

reachable.why: the OS prompt can be shown ONCE on most platforms — a user who declines it has effectively declined permanently, so the cost of asking at a bad moment is the feature, forever. Declining the PRIMING deliberately does not spend the OS prompt

screens.what: Edit display name.

reachable.why: BUILT 2026-07-29, after being refused on "there is no profile data model" — which described a field nothing wrote and concluded it could never be written. gotrue's `updateUser` writes `auth.users.user_metadata`, and the adapter now writes the SAME `full_name` key it already read. The tile watches the identity STREAM rather than the `currentUser` snapshot: a snapshot read compiles, renders, and never rebuilds, so a saved name would go on showing the old value — which is what a save button wired to nothing looks like

screens.what: Language picker, with "follow the device" as a real option.

reachable.why: MaterialApp must READ the override, or the picker stores a choice the app ignores. Was recorded as not-building on 2026-07-29 ("only one locale exists") — which stated the symptom as the cause: nothing blocked adding a second ARB, and the i18n seam had never once run

screens.what: Onboarding carousel. (The SPLASH half is deliberately NOT built — see reachable.why.)

reachable.why: BUILT 2026-07-29 — the ONBOARDING half. The refusal was "content is app-specific", true of the WORDS and false of the MECHANISM: `AppConfig.copy` already existed, so the chassis owns the carousel and each app owns its words. ⚠️ THE COPY FALLS BACK TO l10n, NEVER TO THE KEY — `AppConfig.text(key)` returns the KEY ITSELF when unset and a fresh stamp has no overrides, so a purely config-driven carousel would greet its first user with `onboarding.1.title`. 🔴 The pattern matched here is the EARLY RETURN, because onboarding must be EXEMPT from the auth gate: falling through hands `/onboarding` to the signed-out rule, which sends it to `/sign-in`, and the user never sees onboarding at all — measured on the real redirect log, not reasoned. ⛔ THE SPLASH HALF IS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT AND IS NOT A TODO: a splash is native platform configuration (launch storyboard / launch drawable), so a Dart one renders AFTER the native splash has already shown and adds a SECOND flash rather than removing the first. That refusal was re-checked on 2026-07-29 and stands.

screens.what: The same-app upgrade card in the home body: a labelled, dismissible promotional surface quoting an absolute price derived from the rail.
screens.detail: BUILT 2026-08-10 (research/44 §7 rung 3). SAME-APP ONLY, and that is a store-declaration fact rather than a product preference: Google Play's house-ad trigger is worded "to promote MY OTHER APPS", so a card promoting the app the user is already in matches none of the three YES triggers and carries no ads label (research/44 V2). The cross-app version is a SEPARATE component with a SEPARATE config key, deferred until app #2 exists (rung 6). Prices are ABSOLUTE ONLY — no percentage, no "was", no countdown — because Directive 98/6/EC Art 6a and CJEU C-330/23 require a reduction to be computed against the lowest price of the prior 30 days and this repository holds no price history (V6). The card consults PurchaseCapabilities.canStartCheckout before drawing a buy control and never opens a URL of its own: every offer link resolves to the apex buy surface through the one hosted rail (ADR 038 · V14).

reachable.why: 🔴 THE HARD PART OF THIS ROW IS THAT ITS SHIPPED STATE IS INVISIBLE. features.promo_card_enabled is absent from every config the portfolio serves and an absent feature key reads false, so the card renders a collapsed SizedBox.shrink() in every app today — which is indistinguishable, from the outside, from a surface nobody ever mounted. The two are opposite facts: one is a campaign switched off, the other is the [2]C-6 dead feature. The pattern therefore matches the MOUNT in the stamped home body rather than anything visible, and the chassis property test property: promo-card-fails-closed asserts BOTH halves — mounted-and-zero-height with the flag absent, and a real labelled card with a derived price once the flag is served.

screens.what: Ask for a store review at a good moment.

reachable.why: BUILT 2026-07-29. The refusal was "no users to ask" — an argument about WHEN, not about whether the mechanism can be built, and WHEN turned out to be pure arithmetic over four persisted numbers (`core.ReviewGate`). ⚠️ THE CALL SITE IS THE WHOLE POINT: the gate refuses on almost every launch BY DESIGN, so "nothing happened" is the correct outcome nearly always and a seam with no caller would be invisible for the life of the app. This is the [2]C-6 shape with the best possible camouflage. The prompt itself is OS-drawn and unobservable — neither store reports whether anything appeared — so what is proven is that the request ARRIVES once the gate agrees
